Essraa Daoui, profession enseignante: Essraa Daoui, a Teacher by Profession
« Dans mon cœur, je suis enseignante. Je: “In my heart, I’m a teacher. I’m always teaching children”

“In my heart, I’m a teacher. I’m always teaching children,” Essraa says emphatically. The first thing you notice about her is her vivacity and a passion that shows in a playful spirit, boundless energy and a warmth that comes through even on screen. That dynamism is palpable when she talks about her profession, teaching, a job she isn’t currently practising. The reason: Essraa is on maternity leave. We speak in low voices, so as not to wake the baby, who is almost six months old and asleep. Night fell long ago in Beirut, where the little family is visiting the grandparents.
L’autre raison, c’est la loi 21. Esraa a: The other reason is Bill 21. Essraa earned her degree in preschool and elementary education in 2019. “People only talk about it when it makes the headlines. But it’s a problem all year round,” she says. The debate, a very thorny one, came back to the forefront during the last federal election. Last December, Fatemeh Anvari, a teacher, was removed from her classroom because she wears a hijab. At the beginning of the year, in the middle of a COVID-19 wave, the teacher shortage revived the conversation. Essraa was almost at the finish line, completing her last student teaching placement, when her future was turned upside down. “I was trying to finish quickly, but they passed the law,” she recalls. It was too late. “It isolates you completely,” she says of Bill 21, which affects her deeply. “People whose careers aren’t affected keep moving forward, getting promotions, growing,” the young teacher sums up. When she began her postsecondary studies, Essraa was drawn to physics – she also loved teaching it. Finding she had little affinity with that professional field, she switched to visual arts, an activity that still occupies her today, from drawing to tattooing, which she does in her spare time.
« Ce sont les enfants qui font en sorte: “It’s the children who make me not want to change careers, and who give me hope,” she says. “Bill 21 or not, it’s not a very rewarding job,” she confides. She and her students get along well, even if sometimes, as with anyone, things are harder. “There are kids I don’t click with, and that’s okay. The hijab isn’t the obstacle between them and me; the hijab is never a problem.” While the children don’t make remarks, the looks and behaviour of adults can hurt in schools. “Racism was a source of stress, even before the law. Even during my studies, before the law, there was racism. They exploit you, they infantilize you,” she says of how some colleagues treat her. And from what she says, she is not an isolated case. “I know people who don’t dare talk about it. The teaching staff is almost exclusively white,” she observes. Discrimination is also experienced outside of school. “In Quebec, racism has become legitimate. It’s considered an opinion, and anyone can say it loud and clear,” the young woman believes. She laments that those who once felt uncomfortable in front of a teacher who wears a hijab have won their case. “Their opinion is now legitimate, politically correct.”
Un autre raisonnement fatigue l’enseigna: Another line of reasoning wears the teacher out. “I’m sick of hearing ‘It’s the law, that’s just how it is.’ As if the word ‘law’ meant ‘moral,’ ‘ethical,’ ‘absolute truth.’ There have been very racist, segregationist laws,” the teacher notes. On several occasions, she has been told to take off her hijab to work. “Do you get rid of your beliefs before you walk into work? When you teach, do you become someone who isn’t themselves?” she asks. And watch out for anyone who thinks that wearing a hijab influences children. “With my hijab, I’m not proselytizing, I’m not calling the kids to prayer at recess,” she says in a joking tone that almost masks the gravity of the subject. Essraa stands against anything that is imposed, including religion. “For some people, religion has negative connotations, it’s synonymous with political war, colonization, exploitation, trauma. But you have to understand that it’s not the same experience for everyone.” What would she like to ask decision-makers? “Whether they have friends who wear the hijab, Muslim friends, whether they spend time with any? Or is it only an image they see on TV, built on prejudice? Do they know us?”
Dans quelques jours, Essraa prendra le c: In a few days, Essraa will head home after a stay of several weeks with her family in Lebanon. While she can’t wait to get back, she doesn’t know what awaits her there. “I admit I’m really lost. I have a thousand questions, there’s nothing mapped out in front of me,” says the young mother. She considers herself lucky to have had a child recently. “I have the privilege of having been able to put my career on standby. If I were in career mode, I’d be depressed,” says the teacher. Her maternity leave is coming to an end, and she has to face her new reality. Essraa is considering a professional change and looking at jobs related to teaching. Language being another of her passions, she is thinking about teaching French as a second language to adults and doing tutoring.
Une autre avenue possible est de poursui: Another possible avenue is to continue teaching elementary school in a neighbouring province. “Is it worth leaving my whole life, my whole family, my friends? This is my world, here. Going to Ontario is really sacrificing myself,” she laments. “It’s really destabilizing to make all these changes.” One thing is certain: she will not be becoming a “volunteer parent,” an initiative launched by the Legault government to fill the shortage of school staff, made worse by COVID-19. “It’s ridiculous. There are teachers who are competent, but who can’t teach. The shortage is so bad that they’re ready to have parents, as volunteers, do daycare, that’s how much our work is devalued! Collectively, what are we saying about the teaching profession? Could you replace a doctor like that because there’s a shortage of doctors?”
En attendant, Essraa garde la tête clair: In the meantime, Essraa keeps a clear head by staying away from social media. “I’m protecting myself mentally,” says the woman who was once active there. The days when she answered comments are over; today she focuses her energy elsewhere. “I don’t want to be someone who does nothing but fight all day, every day. I’m capable of doing something else in life.” She wishes for a more peaceful society for everyone, especially for racialized people.
« Les personnes racisées sont continuell: “Racialized people are constantly fighting for their rights, justifying themselves, doing twice the work, while others move forward in life. I wish us a more peaceful world for our hearts, for our minds,” says the woman who, in spite of everything, refuses to be cynical. The conversation ends with the baby crying for his mama. Essraa keeps her radiant smile. After all, as she puts it, she always prefers laughing to crying.
